# Canon brief

> Research status: READY  
> Resolution owner: coordinator  
> Authority conflict: none  
> User ruling required: no

## Hard constraints

- Fulfill the captured prompt contract: 2,500–4,000 words; close second person centered on an unnamed viewpoint character; past tense; Teen-rated suspense; a hooded stranger sitting beside the viewpoint character at a bar; the invitation appearing verbatim; an expected party of companions; the proposed game driving the central conflict; the arriving party becoming materially significant; and a resolved outcome with a real cost. Do not use an unearned rescue, dream reset, or chapter-fragment ending. (`stories/a-friendly-little-game/00-prompt.md` — `## Verbatim writing prompt`, `## Story controls`, `## Assumptions`, `## Completion tests`)
- The exact spoken invitation is: “While we wait for the rest of your party to arrive, would you like to partake in a friendly little game?” The wording must not be silently corrected or paraphrased. (`stories/a-friendly-little-game/00-prompt.md` — `## Verbatim writing prompt`)
- Keep the viewpoint character unnamed. A persistent role, epithet, title, nickname, or alias used in place of a personal name would still be character-facing production naming and would require validation. (`stories/a-friendly-little-game/00-prompt.md` — `## Story controls`; `stories/NAMES.md` — `## Rules`)
- “Party” means expected companions, not a political organization. Their significance must be dramatized through their arrival, choices, relationships, capabilities, or exposure to the game—not merely explained after the outcome. (`stories/a-friendly-little-game/00-prompt.md` — `## Assumptions`, `## Story controls`)
- Place the new bar and locality within the shared physical world, preferably in an unnamed era and region. Do not declare a disconnected universe merely to avoid continuity. Other dimensions may exist, but canon does not require one here; introducing one would be a new, tightly bounded cosmological proposal rather than established lore. (`universe/premise.md` — `## The deep-time shared world`; `universe/locations.md` — `## The world across eras`)
- Magic, technology, and divinity are cultural labels for real underlying systems, not universal objective categories. A new game may be mundane, technological, magical, hybrid, or culturally misclassified, but its observed behavior must remain internally coherent. (`universe/rules.md` — `## System categories`)
- Only life can use magic. Cards, dice, cups, coins, boards, tables, contracts, bar fixtures, and other nonliving components may store, focus, transmit, display, or shape living-supplied magic, or perform established nonmagical automation, but may not independently cast magic. If any component is conscious or person-like, establish its life and preserve its agency and moral status. (`universe/rules.md` — `## Living agency and magic`; `universe/style-guide.md` — `## Personhood and moral consequence`)
- Winning, losing, wagering, pain, desire, sacrifice, honesty, consent, and cost have no universal magical force. If one affects this game mechanically, define a bounded local mechanism with a living supplier or user, access condition, comprehensible turn structure, limits, failure behavior, and consequences. (`universe/rules.md` — `## Costs, desire, and local mechanisms`)
- Names are not universally magical. The stranger cannot know, bind, summon, identify, or control the party merely through names unless a new local mechanism establishes exactly how; resemblance to Ravel’s identity system or the Rollcaller does not supply that mechanism. (`universe/rules.md` — `## Names and identity binding`, `## Regent three-line identity infrastructure`, `## Rollcaller mimicry and short-term containment`)
- Deception may be the stranger’s wrongdoing and may compromise the viewpoint character’s consent. The story must not convert coerced, uninformed, or manipulated participation into moral authorization merely because the stranger calls it a game or states a rule. Ethical consequences remain real even where a local mechanism recognizes a move. (`universe/rules.md` — `## Costs, desire, and local mechanisms`; `universe/style-guide.md` — `## Personhood and moral consequence`)
- The viewpoint character cannot legitimately wager absent companions’ bodies, memories, identities, freedom, property, or future choices without their authority. The stranger may threaten or attempt such a transfer, and the viewpoint character may make an unethical choice, but the narrative must recognize the coercion and resulting responsibility. (`stories/the-future-that-refused-us/05-story.md` — `# The Future That Refused Us`; `stories/the-last-thing-i-could-fix/05-story.md` — `# The Last Thing I Could Fix`)
- A game result cannot itself create ownership, romantic consent, bodily access, permanent service, or a relationship. Lacebridge’s local courtesy-bout precedent makes even a mutually negotiated courtship stake grant only an invitation that may be declined; it is not a universal game law, but it is a relevant personhood boundary. (`universe/factions.md` — `## Lacebridge civic blade-yard practice`; `stories/the-courtesy-of-blades/05-story.md` — `# The Courtesy of Blades`)
- Do not infer a crossover, common maker, or shared mechanism from cards, bargains, hidden rules, hoods, strangers, bars, contracts, wagers, copper, repeated imagery, or similar story shapes. (`universe/rules.md` — `## Artifacts, motifs, and folklore`; `universe/style-guide.md` — `## Continuity and evidence discipline`)
- Preserve the Teen ceiling: peril and restrained violence are permitted, but violence and horror remain non-graphic and consequence-centered; sexual content is excluded by the prompt and project ceiling. (`stories/a-friendly-little-game/00-prompt.md` — `## Story controls`; `universe/style-guide.md` — `## Audience and content boundaries`)

## Relevant established context and precedents

- Independent audience entry points are normal. The story needs no crossover, famous artifact, named era, recurring faction, or exposition about the full cosmology. An ordinary-looking bar with one bounded speculative intrusion is canon-compatible. (`universe/premise.md` — `## Knowledge and connection`; `universe/style-guide.md` — `## Tonal range, scale, and connection`)
- Canon establishes no universal tavern network, supernatural bar custom, adventuring-party structure, game tradition, wager law, hooded order, or stranger taxonomy. Familiar fantasy or modern social forms may be used locally without importing an external game ruleset.
- *The Trouble With Tuesdays* establishes only that Eli Fenwick’s grandfather won one copper watch in a card game and signed a witnessed napkin whose local agreement bound ownership into his living bloodline and restricted the Time-title bearer. The opponent’s reported identity is unreliable, the game itself is unexplained, and the event establishes no universal card, wager, contract, saint, bloodline, or divine law. A new game must not casually identify its stranger, contract, or prize with that incident. (`universe/rules.md` — `## Fenwick watch ownership contract and audit`; `stories/the-trouble-with-tuesdays/05-story.md` — `# The Trouble With Tuesdays`)
- *The Courtesy of Blades* is the clearest admitted contest precedent: transparent mundane rules, a qualified official, surrender and stoppage, truthful self-calls, and a tightly limited personal stake. It supports readable rules and bounded stakes but creates a structural collision risk if the new story becomes another formal contest whose winner earns an invitation or date. (`universe/factions.md` — `## Lacebridge civic blade-yard practice`; `universe/timeline.md` — `## Undated Lacebridge trial and courtesy bout`)
- *The Last Bus to Briar Hill* establishes a living Briar Host that presents bounded tests and cached sensory lures, while a living route-tender supplies power to a nonliving bus. Its false messages, copied dead loved one, three request stops, current-reply verification, sunrise return, and promise-completion language are specific to that story. A living game host is possible, but those tests and transit structure must not be repeated or treated as a general rule. (`stories/the-last-bus-to-briar-hill/05-story.md` — `# The Last Bus to Briar Hill`)
- *The Wrong Side of the Part* establishes one nonliving wig that focuses its living wearer’s heat, pulse, and self-conception, intensifies a denied posture, and releases when the wearer states an unwanted truth. It preserves the wearer’s memory and responsibility. A game that changes temperament or ends when the player confesses a buried truth would risk closely repeating that mechanism and emotional proof. (`stories/the-wrong-side-of-the-part/05-story.md` — `# The Wrong Side of the Part`)
- *Realms* establishes one living market whose prices respond locally to expressed desire and one offered relational-memory contract. Cal refuses that contract, so its represented effect is not demonstrated. A game may have emotional or memory stakes, but desire pricing, shame-gated entry, relational-memory erasure, and Deepmarket imagery belong to that bounded system. (`universe/rules.md` — `## Deepmarket desire pricing and stated memory toll`, `## Deepmarket name access, shame gate, and offered memory contract`; `stories/realms/05-story.md` — `# Realms`)
- *A Place for the Living* treats an undisclosed partner audition and the coerced continuation of a guest’s visit as ethical violations despite sincere family motives and a real local tradition. A secret test of the viewpoint character’s worthiness may be depicted, but calling it hospitality or play does not make the ambush fair. (`stories/a-place-for-the-living/05-story.md` — `# A Place for the Living`)
- *The Future That Refused Us* explicitly condemns a plan whose informed volunteers appeared to stake their own lives while uninformed families actually carried the uncertainty. *The Last Thing I Could Fix* similarly rejects protection that covertly transfers harm through another person’s protective reflex. These are strong consequence precedents if the stranger’s apparent wager externalizes its cost onto the arriving party. (`stories/the-future-that-refused-us/05-story.md` — `# The Future That Refused Us`; `stories/the-last-thing-i-could-fix/05-story.md` — `# The Last Thing I Could Fix`)
- *The Attendance Ledger* establishes a living Rollcaller that exploits ordinary records, imitation, attention, and cumulative observation to expose concealed identities. If the game asks the viewpoint character to name, describe, betray, or predict companions, avoid copied voice orders, attendance records, school exposure, filament-linked equipment, and the Rollcaller identity-hunt structure. (`universe/rules.md` — `## Rollcaller mimicry and short-term containment`; `stories/the-attendance-ledger/05-story.md` — `# The Attendance Ledger`)
- No admitted story establishes this bar, stranger, party, game, or their relationship. Their absence is omission, not evidence that any proposed mechanism already belongs to canon.

## Conflicts and collision risks

- **Contradiction:** None in the captured prompt. The story can proceed without a canon ruling.
- **Omission, not contradiction:** Canon does not identify the unnamed viewpoint character, hooded stranger, party members, bartender, patrons, bar, era, locality, or reason for the party’s delayed arrival.
- **Omission, not contradiction:** Canon does not define the game’s format, rules, rounds, apparent stakes, real stakes, deception, power source, victory condition, refusal condition, cost, or aftermath.
- **Omission, not contradiction:** Canon does not establish that a hood conceals species, identity, divinity, undeath, or magical power. It may be ordinary clothing.
- **Omission, not contradiction:** Canon does not determine whether the party is an adventuring company, expedition, friend group, work team, family, rescue unit, or another group of companions.
- **Conditional contradiction:** Making the game’s cards, dice, board, contract, drinks, or table independent magic users while leaving them nonliving would contradict `Living agency and magic`.
- **Conditional contradiction:** Treating desire, pain, sacrifice, truth, consent, a wager, a spoken promise, or a signed score as universally operative magic would contradict the locality rule.
- **Conditional contradiction:** Giving the stranger universal access to names, memories, futures, guilt, or party members without a defined bounded mechanism would exceed authority and may contradict established locality limits.
- **Conditional contradiction:** Treating absent companions as validly bound by the viewpoint character’s unilateral wager would violate established personhood and consequence boundaries.
- **Conditional contradiction:** Calling the stranger objectively divine without the continuing conjunction of worship, power, and authority would contradict the godhood taxonomy. A local title or belief does not prove godhood. (`universe/rules.md` — `## Divinity`)
- **Structural collision:** A card game that transfers a bloodline-bound time artifact through a witnessed informal contract would closely repeat the Fenwick watch provenance.
- **Structural collision:** A sequence of fair-seeming tests administered by a living host, including copied messages, false dead loved ones, verification from outside the boundary, and a timed return, would closely repeat Briar Hill.
- **Structural collision:** A magical object that amplifies the viewpoint character’s repressed opposite until an unwanted truth is spoken would closely repeat *The Wrong Side of the Part*.
- **Structural collision:** A desire-priced memory bargain, shame-gated venue, or erasure of companions’ memories of the player would closely repeat Deepmarket.
- **Structural collision:** A regulated duel or game whose winner receives only an invitation would closely repeat Lacebridge’s courtesy-bout resolution.
- **Authority conflict:** None among current `LOCKED`/`CANON` entries and the admitted canon stories relevant to this prompt.

## Unknowns

- The era, region, settlement, culture, legal environment, and relation to every established location.
- Whether the bar is contemporary-looking, historical, fantasy-coded, itinerant, hidden, or ordinary apart from the stranger.
- The viewpoint character’s age, gender, pronouns, species, occupation, party role, private fear, current objective, and reason for arriving before the others.
- The hooded stranger’s age, gender, pronouns beyond the prompt’s neutral reference, species, life status, motive, knowledge, honesty, powers, limits, and reason for choosing this player.
- Whether the stranger caused, predicted, merely noticed, or has no control over the party’s delayed arrival.
- The number of companions, their relationships to the viewpoint character, their reason for meeting, and whether they arrive together or in stages.
- Whether the party knows about the stranger or game before arriving.
- Why the viewpoint character accepts instead of refusing, leaving, warning the party, or involving the bartender.
- The game’s physical form, number of rounds, legal moves, information available to each participant, stop conditions, cheating conditions, and apparent victory condition.
- What is deceptive: the stranger’s identity, the opponent, the object of play, the meaning of a move, the source of information, the actual stake, or who is being tested.
- Whether any mechanism is magical, technological, biological, divine, social, fraudulent, or mixed.
- The living user or supplier behind every magical effect and the precise role of any nonliving game component.
- What the viewpoint character believes they can wager and what authority they actually possess.
- The immediate and lasting cost of winning, losing, refusing, cheating, or exposing the deception.
- How the arriving companions exercise independent choices rather than functioning only as prizes, hostages, pieces, or rescue machinery.
- What emotionally satisfying turn resolves both the game and the viewpoint character’s relationship to the party.
- All character-facing names, aliases, titles used as names, group names, named game terms, named objects, and person-like entities.

These are omissions and planning questions, not missing canon to be filled by this brief.

## Safe local invention space

- Create a new bar or tavern in an unnamed locality and era of the shared physical world. It may be mundane except for one bounded speculative participant or mechanism.
- Keep the viewpoint character unnamed while giving them a clear party role, emotional fault line, and reason to be alone early.
- Create an original living hooded stranger. The hood may conceal an ordinary face, a culturally unfamiliar person, a transformed body, a constructed living person, or another locally defined identity; none of those options is established canon.
- Create an original group of companions with distinct relationships, capabilities, boundaries, and reasons for arriving. They need not form a recurring institution.
- Use cards, dice, stones, cups, coins, marked coasters, questions, gestures, stories, or another compact bar-table format. Nonliving components may display or focus living-supplied power without becoming independent magic users.
- Make the deception legible in retrospect. It may exploit equivocal wording, unequal information, social assumptions, or a concealed opponent, but the resolution should not depend on an arbitrary rule invented after the decisive move.
- Let the viewpoint character risk only something they can actually choose—time, money, information about themself, a promise they can personally fulfill, temporary pain, public embarrassment, or another bounded personal cost. If the stranger attempts to claim companions as stakes, frame that as coercion or fraud rather than legitimate ownership.
- Make the party’s arrival part of the game’s causal structure: each arrival may invalidate an assumption, reveal withheld context, refuse a claimed stake, make a new choice, or force the viewpoint character to choose between winning and protecting trust.
- The party may help, but the viewpoint character should make the decisive choice that resolves the invitation they accepted. This avoids an unearned rescue while preserving the party’s significance.
- A mundane con with one speculative consequence is viable. The game itself need not be magical if the stranger, bar, party, or cost supplies the speculative element.
- If memory, identity, prediction, binding, transformation, or copied perception is used, define a new local mechanism and differentiate it from Deepmarket, the Fenwick watch, Ravel, the Rollcaller, Briar Hill, and the truth-trigger wig.
- Keep any proposed canon addition narrow: these observed people, this bar, this specific game, and its demonstrated limits. Do not generalize one incident into a universal class of hooded strangers or supernatural games.

## Concrete canon recommendation

Proceed with an original standalone bar in an unnamed era, an unnamed viewpoint character who arrived before their companions, and a living stranger running one bounded social game through non-agentic table pieces.

The safest central design is a game that appears to test prediction or loyalty but actually exposes what authority the viewpoint character assumes over the absent party. The stranger may exploit ambiguity or attempt to convert statements about companions into stakes, while the arriving companions independently reject, confirm, or complicate those statements. The viewpoint character should resolve the game through a costly choice of their own rather than by successfully wagering someone else.

Keep the mechanism distinct from existing precedents: no bloodline timepiece or napkin contract, no desire-priced memory erasure, no three-stop glamour trial, no copied dead loved one, no truth-trigger personality inversion, and no date-as-prize courtesy bout.

## Name constraints

- The viewpoint character must remain unnamed under the prompt contract. Avoid revealing a personal name in dialogue, narration, records, scorecards, or the final turn.
- Lowercase `the hooded stranger`, `the stranger`, `the bartender`, and ordinary party-role nouns may remain descriptions. If `Stranger`, `Dealer`, `Gamekeeper`, `Bartender`, or another role becomes a persistent proper title or standalone identity, it must be validated and registered.
- Every party member’s full name, given name, mononym, nickname, alias, title used as a name, and group name must be checked against the complete current registry before drafting.
- Do not name the companion group `the Quiet Party` or `Quiet Party`. Those forms remain reserved production memory from a removed story version even though they establish no canon.
- Closely related removed-version reservations also remain unavailable for casual reuse: `Veda Crake`, `Veda`, `Osket Firth`, `Osket`, `Pim Fallow`, `Pim`, `Merrit Loam`, and `Merrit`.
- Avoid reusing test-host and night-guide identities from the closest precedent: `the Briar Host`, `Briar Host`, `Maude Dallow`, `Maude`, and `Ms. Dallow`.
- Avoid `the Goddess of Time`, `Goddess of Time`, and `Time` for the stranger, and do not turn the lowercase reported phrase `minor saint of bad decisions` into a new proper identity without an intentional continuity decision.
- Avoid `the Rollcaller` / `Rollcaller`, particularly if the game concerns companions’ names or concealed identities.
- Avoid `Jasper Renlow`, `Jasper`, `Fiora Halwick`, `Fiora`, and `Quade` if the game is contest- or wager-centered; those forms identify the Lacebridge principals.
- `stories/NAMES.md` currently reports no unresolved collisions, but canon, candidate, in-progress, abandoned, and unreleased historical reservations remain searchable. Absence from canon does not release a reserved production name.
- Check exact matches, aliases, close spellings, reversals, sound-alikes, and confusable silhouettes. Deliberate reuse requires a story-significant reason, an identity relationship where applicable, and clear reader disambiguation. This prompt supplies no reason for reuse.
- Check any named game, magical technique, contract, bar, faction, or speculative system against `universe/glossary.md` and existing location/faction terminology even when it is not a character-facing name.

## Required later checks

- **Story architect:** Preserve close second person, past tense, the unnamed viewpoint, Teen ceiling, exact invitation, bar setting, expected companions, resolved game, and consequential cost.
- **Story architect:** Define why the viewpoint character arrives first, why the party is delayed, why the stranger knows they are expected, and which facts are genuine rather than assumed.
- **Story architect:** Produce a compact game specification: physical components, participants, turns, information, apparent objective, actual objective, legal moves, refusal and stopping behavior, deception, win/loss conditions, and costs.
- **Story architect:** Create a stake-authority map distinguishing what the viewpoint character can choose from what belongs to each absent companion.
- **Story architect:** Give every companion an independent goal and at least one consequential choice on arrival; do not design them solely as prizes, hostages, pieces, or rescuers.
- **Story architect:** Ensure the viewpoint character’s final choice resolves the accepted game while the party’s arrival changes its meaning or available options.
- **Story architect:** Identify every living magical user or supplier, every nonliving focus, every limit, and every failure state.
- **Story architect:** Differentiate the plot from the Fenwick card-game contract, Lacebridge wager, Briar Host tests, Deepmarket bargains, Rollcaller identity hunt, and truth-trigger wig.
- **Coordinator:** Validate and register every planned companion name, stranger name or stable title, bartender or patron name, group name, named animal, named object treated as person-like, and person-like game entity. Preserve the narrator’s unnamed status.
- **Prose writer:** Include the invitation verbatim and make the stranger physically sit beside the viewpoint character at the bar.
- **Prose writer:** Maintain second-person reference without accidentally naming the viewpoint character through dialogue, scorekeeping, paperwork, or exposition.
- **Prose writer:** Make each game round understandable enough that suspense arises from inference and deception rather than withheld causality.
- **Prose writer:** Foreshadow the actual meaning of the decisive move and allow the final turn to recontextualize earlier rounds.
- **Prose writer:** Dramatize the party’s arrival on page and give it causal weight. Do not resolve the game before the companions matter.
- **Prose writer:** Preserve accountability if the viewpoint character betrays confidence, volunteers another person’s stakes, or chooses to continue after recognizing manipulation.
- **Prose writer:** Show the cost after the outcome; do not erase injury, lost trust, lost time, debt, disclosure, or another consequence in the final paragraph.
- **Continuity critic:** Check for autonomous nonliving magic, universal wager or contract law, universal truth/name/memory access, unsupported prophecy, objective godhood without the required conjunction, or separate-world language.
- **Continuity critic:** Check whether the stranger’s deception makes consent compromised and whether the narrative treats that honestly.
- **Continuity critic:** Check that no rule binds absent companions merely because the viewpoint character described, predicted, named, or wagered them.
- **Continuity critic:** Compare the completed plot specifically against *The Trouble With Tuesdays*, *The Last Bus to Briar Hill*, *The Wrong Side of the Part*, *Realms*, *The Courtesy of Blades*, *The Future That Refused Us*, and *The Last Thing I Could Fix*.
- **Continuity critic:** Reject an arbitrary hidden-rule victory, dream reset, sudden unrelated rescue, passive arriving party, or ending that leaves either the game or its cost unresolved.
- **Story editor:** Keep final canon-delta claims local to observed people, place, game, and mechanism. Do not propose a universal order of game-playing strangers, tavern network, wager metaphysics, or contract law.
- **Final name gate:** Re-extract every final character-facing form and reconcile it against the current registry, including any title or role promoted into a proper identity.

## Authority and evidence audit

The remaining admitted stories create no additional bar, party, or game conflict.
